## Ozone layer

The ozone layer sits in the lower stratosphere (roughly 15–35 km above Earth) and is defined by an unusually high concentration of ozone relative to the rest of the atmosphere. Peak ozone there reaches 8–15 parts per million, compared with about 0.3 ppm averaged over the whole atmosphere.[1]{c1}

Its compositional significance is as a UV shield: it absorbs 97–99% of the Sun's medium-frequency ultraviolet light (roughly 200–315 nm), which would otherwise potentially damage exposed life near the surface.[1]{c2}

The layer is also a product of atmospheric composition. Ultraviolet light strikes O2 molecules, splitting them into atomic oxygen that then combines with unbroken O2 to create ozone — the ozone–oxygen cycle.[1]{c3} Accordingly, the layer formed about 500 million years ago, when the Neoproterozoic oxygenation event brought atmospheric oxygen to about 20%.[1]{c4}

Composition cuts both ways: in 1985, atmospheric research revealed the layer was being depleted by industrial chemicals, mainly CFCs.[1]{c5} Concerns over the resulting increase in UV led to bans on these chemicals, and the latest evidence is that depletion has slowed or stopped.

## Photosynthesis

Oxygenic photosynthesis — the usual meaning of the term — releases oxygen as a byproduct of splitting water.[2]{c6} This makes photosynthesis a direct driver of atmospheric composition: it plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of Earth's atmosphere, while also supplying most of the biological energy necessary for complex life.[2]{c7}

Historically, the excess oxygen produced by cyanobacteria contributed directly to the oxygenation of the Earth, which rendered the evolution of complex life possible.[2]{c8} (Some organisms also carry out anoxygenic photosynthesis, which does not release oxygen.)

## How the two connect

Photosynthesis maintains the O2 content of the atmosphere, and UV-driven chemistry converts some of that O2 into the stratospheric ozone that constitutes the ozone layer. The ozone layer is thus a downstream consequence of photosynthetic oxygenation — and, in turn, it shields exposed life near the surface from damaging UV radiation. The CFC episode showed how sensitive this compositional system is to change, and how policy intervention (bans) can allow it to recover.
